strengths: The method addresses a useful computer vision problem: scalable dataset distillation through representative teacher features and class-specific BatchNorm statistics, without differentiating through student training.

Table I reports consistent improvements over a strengthened, reproduced SRe2L baseline. On ImageNet-1K, accuracy increases from 54.4% to 57.6% at 50 images per class and from 58.3% to 60.7% at 100 images per class.

Experiments cover three datasets and several compression budgets, with repeated evaluations, component ablations, regularization sensitivity, and transfer to additional architectures. Table II demonstrates useful transfer to larger ResNets.

The manuscript clearly acknowledges its dependence on SRe2L and credits the existing Wasserstein algorithms and POT library. Reporting the improved baseline and supplying synthesis hyperparameters strengthens experimental transparency.
weaknesses: The central novelty relative to ordinary feature clustering is not established. Equation (4) approximates one empirical distribution with a smaller support. With squared Euclidean cost and freely optimized atom masses, its unregularized form is exactly the k-means/vector-quantization objective. This relationship requires analysis and a direct clustering baseline; a matched feature-space MMD comparison would also help substantiate the claimed advantage of Wasserstein matching.

The ablations provide limited support for attributing the gains specifically to Wasserstein matching. At 10 images per class, CE plus class-specific BatchNorm without barycenter matching already achieves 64.0/41.3/37.4%, versus 64.8/41.8/38.2% for the full method. Holding CE and BatchNorm fixed, adding barycenter matching changes accuracy by -0.1/+0.8/+0.5 percentage points. Most improvement therefore comes from class-specific BatchNorm in this setting, while the larger-budget gains lack corresponding ablations.

The connection between the optimized distribution and the delivered training set is incomplete. Equation (3) and the barycenter algorithms learn atom masses, but Algorithm 1 returns only images, and downstream sampling or loss weighting using those masses is unspecified. Matching each support point once through Equation (5) does not establish that training uses the weighted distribution optimized in Equation (4).

Important details of the central solver remain ambiguous. The text states that entropic regularization is used, while the appendix presents unregularized transport primal and dual problems. The entropy coefficient, support initialization, and concrete stopping criteria are not supplied, limiting reproducibility and obscuring which objective produced the results.

The efficiency claims exceed the measurements provided. Table IV reports only the proposed method's per-update synthesis cost on 64×64 ImageNette, without comparative timings or accounting for feature extraction and transport computation. The approximately 14-hour ImageNet run demonstrates feasibility, but does not establish that the method preserves the computational advantages of existing distribution-matching approaches.
